title: The Supreme Court Recognizes the Danger of Trump’s Election Plan
summary: Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night, nor Donald Trump will stop the United States Postal Service from delivering mail-in ballots in the coming midterm elections. Tonight, the Supreme Court handed down an emergency ruling blocking the Trump administration from implementing a new poli...
content:
Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night, nor Donald Trump will stop the United States Postal Service from delivering mail-in ballots in the coming midterm elections. Tonight, the Supreme Court handed down an emergency ruling blocking the Trump administration from implementing a new policy that would have made mail-in voting so onerous as to be effectively impossible for election officials to administer. The Court’s decision spares those officials from pointless chaos—and voters from potentially widespread disenfranchisement.

In the United States, election administration is carried out by a patchwork of local officials, working state-by-state across over roughly 10,000 different jurisdictions. Usually, USPS’s role in elections is clear: The Postal Service transports mail ballots to voters from state and local election offices; if voters return their ballots by mail, USPS takes care of that, too. The nature of this responsibility has evolved in recent years, particularly during the pandemic, as many states shifted toward encouraging voting by mail. The Trump administration looked at this system, which has been popular among voters, and decided to cause havoc by imposing new and arduous criteria for election officials to meet before the USPS would commit to mailing ballots.

A number of states and several nonprofits, along with the Democratic Party, quickly brought legal challenges. Before the Court resolved the matter tonight, the cases zagged madly among district and appellate courts, then up to the Supreme Court and back down again. Many judges were skeptical both of the legal basis for the rule and of the speed at which the administration was attempting to implement it, with less than two months to go before the election.

But despite this broad agreement in the lower courts, experts were uncertain how the Supreme Court would handle the case. The Court’s past friendliness toward even the most legally dubious of Trump’s policies cast into doubt whether the justices would stand against his efforts here, especially after the Court rejected an earlier iteration of the challenge on the grounds that it had been premature. “The Supreme Court has made law totally unpredictable,” the election-law expert Justin Levitt told me last week, while the country waited for the justices to rule. “In a normal world, there would be a zero percent chance” that the Court would allow the USPS rule to go into effect. And yet, he went on, “We don’t live in a normal world anymore.”

Our world is still not a normal one. But this time, a majority of justices on the Supreme Court decided not to make it worse. In a terse, unsigned paragraph, the Court declared that the Trump administration had failed both to make its case on the law and to show that a ruling in Trump’s favor would not upend the upcoming elections. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in a brief concurrence, indicated that the Postal Service’s plan might have had firm legal grounding, but agreed to block the policy because “state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”

That final part of his assessment is obviously correct. USPS’s plan would have required election officials to upload lists of eligible voters through a Postal Service “portal”—yet the government has given no indication that the portal is operational. USPS would also have required election officials to receive Postal Service approval for the design of their ballot envelopes, but officials have already printed their ballot envelopes and do not have money or time to create new designs. Last week, a Tallahassee, Florida, paper reported that USPS rejected the envelope designs submitted by Florida’s Leon County on the grounds that the return address was 0.014 inches too close to other text on the envelope—about the thickness of four sheets of paper.

Election administrators prepare to send out ballots far in advance, and if the USPS rule had gone into effect, election officials might have found themselves unable to count on the Postal Service to mail ballots at all. However conservative the Supreme Court is, “there aren’t five votes for abject chaos,” Levitt wrote to me after the ruling.

Still, Justices Samuel Alito and Justice Clarence Thomas, the pair on the Court who most reliably tilt toward Trump, would have allowed the USPS plan to go forward. Alito’s dissent is strikingly unconcerned with the potential risks to the midterms if the Postal Service were to refuse to mail ballots, noting only that 12 states (all Republican-led) have “asserted that compliance at this time is practicable.” (Local election officials in some of those states disagreed with that assessment in their own court filings, but Alito does not address this.) Moreover, the federal government’s interest in detecting “election fraud” is compelling, Alito declares. As for the last-minute dash to shake up the midterms, Alito manages to blame not the government but the plaintiffs, the lower courts, and even his own colleagues on the bench for the litigation that—he claims—delayed the USPS from finalizing its rule.

In a blog post, the UCLA law professor and election scholar Rick Hasen deemed Alito’s dissent “disingenuous.” Among other things, USPS continued working on the rule during the course of the litigation over the summer. And even if the Postal Service had finished the planning process earlier in the summer, state and local jurisdictions still might not have had enough time to rework their envelopes to comply.

Fortunately, officials won’t need to scramble to submit envelope designs to the USPS to be measured down to fractions of an inch, or upload voter names into a portal that doesn’t exist. Election workers will likely face plenty of challenges in the month and a half before the midterms. Mailing ballots, though, will not be among them.

title: ‘The Flood is the Point’

content:
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Donald Trump loves a deal, even if, at times, it’s just the idea of a deal. The president’s trade dispute with Canada continues to drive one of America’s closest allies into a closer relationship with its chief competition. Although Trump is insisting that “Canada wants to make a deal very badly,” there is very little evidence that’s true, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney—enjoying broad national approval for his combative response to the American leader—looks to strengthen its alliances in Europe and Asia.

Meanwhile, AI leaders are publicly calling for a slowdown. That was the gist of the message delivered by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei this weekend in an essay warning that the technological advances of AI are outpacing the ability to ensure that they are safe. His concerns were echoed by some of the biggest names in tech—OpenAI leader Sam Altman and Elon Musk.

But the president saw something else in their warnings: “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” Trump wrote on his social-media site this morning.

This week on Radio Atlantic, my colleagues Ashley Parker and Tom Nichols join me to discuss the president’s trade war with Canada, the Trump-centric Republican midterm convention in Dallas, and whether an aging Congress can regulate AI.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Ashley Parker: To be somewhat fair to Trump, or to anyone, is that this is just fundamentally incredibly complex. If you’ve ever watched these members of Congress—which is basically a gerontocracy—try to get to the bottom of Snapchat or Instagram or social media with teens, right, it’s like they’re speaking a foreign language, and those are table stakes, right? AI is a million times more complicated than posting a problematic video on YouTube or Instagram.

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris. Congress is back on Capitol Hill for the last time before the midterm elections, and they have a lot to think about—the burgeoning trade war with Canada and warnings from tech CEOs about the dangers of unregulated AI, among other things.

And when those lawmakers return to the campaign trail for the final stretch, the ones in competitive districts may have some company—members of the president’s Cabinet.

With me to discuss the news of the week are my colleagues Ashley Parker and Tom Nichols. Let’s get to questions.

Welcome to the show.

Parker: Thanks for having us.

Tom Nichols: Thanks, Adam.

Harris: Ashley, I want to start with you because you had a story that ran recently about something that people I think have become a little bit desensitized to, and that’s the potential violations of the Hatch Act, which limits the partisan political activities of federal employees. You and our colleague Michael Scherer reported on a competition among the Cabinet secretaries to travel to competitive electoral districts. Can you sort of walk us through that reporting?

Parker: Sure. So the first way we heard about this competition, which was not public, was almost inadvertently. We were speaking with a Cabinet secretary who said that there was an event in New York that they had kind of wanted to attend, but had declined because they didn’t want to get docked points in the competition. And we were immediately like, What competition?

And so it turns out that there is this unofficial travel competition in the Trump White House. It’s overseen by a woman named Meghan Bauer, who basically coordinates with all of the Cabinet secretaries, officially running between Memorial Day and Labor Day. And basically the goal is to encourage Cabinet officials, Cabinet secretaries to travel the country, particularly to swing districts or swing states that are competitive in the midterms. And each time they go to one of these areas, they get a point. And what this Cabinet official was worried about was losing points, although the official was mistaken. When we began reporting, many officials at the White House told us, Nobody ever loses points; you only accrue points. And they even said, Look, if someone is heading to New York to, say, do a hit on CNN, to talk about Trump’s policies, that still would count as a point.

Harris: We can talk about it in point systems, but we should also think of it in terms of the law, right? Like, is this a Hatch Act violation?

Parker: So, no, not inherently, but it brings Cabinet officials potentially quite close to the line, and it’s something they need to be careful of. So just to put it in a little historical perspective, this general thing of wanting your top officials, your Cabinet officials, out in the country selling the president’s policies, especially in the run-up to a midterm election, is incredibly common. [George W.] Bush did it; [Barack] Obama did it; [Joe] Biden did it.

And Biden, I remember, the most in-demand Cabinet official at the time, when he was president in the run-up to the midterms, was Pete Buttigieg. So Cabinet officials can go and they can talk about—especially if it’s related to their jobs, an agriculture secretary, for instance, or let’s just take Pete Buttigieg for an example. Pete Buttigieg could travel the country and talk about how this stimulus package that Biden and Democrats helped to pass had brought a bridge to your district, had brought new roads to your state, was responsible for huge construction projects over here that had created jobs. That’s all totally fine and not a Hatch Act violation.

If it becomes more overtly political—showing up in a district at a campaign stop with, say, a Senate candidate and just saying, Hey, vote for Ken Paxton in Texas—that is where you get into problems. And the Trump officials, some of them have gotten into problems.

Harris: Tom, how do you process the sort of flood, the stream of controversy, that comes from the administration?

Nichols: Well, I actually am intimately familiar with the Hatch Act because people filed complaints against me constantly when I was a federal employee, before I came to The Atlantic. I was a professor at the Naval War College, which meant I was a Defense Department employee, but I wrote articles and I wrote op-eds and I spoke my mind. And I always finish with, These are my personal views, speaking as an American citizen, et cetera, et cetera.

So I think Ashley’s description of, boy, right up to the line, is a great way to think of it. And the larger point, I think, is that, Adam, like you asked: Why does this happen? How do we cope with this flood? And I think that the flood is the point. The fire hose is the point, because at some point, you just sort of throw up your hands and say, Which of these, you know, 9 million things?

It used to be that, even in the first Trump term, somebody getting hit with a Hatch Act violation was a big deal. I mean, it made the news. Kellyanne Conway, there were couple of other—

Parker: Yeah, I remember the Kellyanne Conway one. And it stood out, right?

Nichols: Yeah, right. Because it was rare. And because it was so obvious. And I think it’s part of that whole fire-hosing strategy, where you just sit back and say, Okay, fine. I give up, because tomorrow there will be something else. And then the Hatch Act will seem relatively minor by comparison.

Parker: I was thinking about this as I was biking into work today, which is, if you even just look at today’s news, Hatch Act violations are comparatively quaint, right? I mean, I’m biking in, I see that ProPublica has reported that a Russian oligarch who’s very close to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin bankrolled Donald Trump Jr.’s intimate wedding a few months ago. And amid all these warnings that AI is going to kill us in a doomsday scenario, President Trump came out and said, We’re not slowing down; there’s no regulations. So if a Cabinet official says, Hey, vote for this Republican congressman, in the panoply of things that watchdog groups are worrying about, it’s not top of the list, to be frank.

Nichols: I know the broken-windows theory of crime has been more or less discredited, but there is a kind of feeling of this of, It starts with the Hatch Act. The Hatch Act is like turnstile jumping in the subway, but enough people do it enough times and pretty soon, you know, it’s people shooting at each other in the streets and robbing banks. And it kind of feels that way now. There are no guardrails.

I mean, the story that Ashley just mentioned, about Don Jr.’s wedding. Again, if you were a federal employee, if you even talked to a Russian, that was paperwork right there. I could not imagine saying, Oh yeah, and by the way, he paid for my wedding. But we’ve just kind of gotten used to it.

Harris: Republicans gathered in Dallas, Texas, last week for a sort of unusual midterm convention. What did we learn about where Republicans are right now, if anything, coming out of that convention?

Nichols: We learned that the party belongs to Donald Trump and that thousands of people will repeat every word he says if he tells them to. That, I think, tells you everything you need to know—about the party, not about the election, but about the party.

Parker: I think that’s about right, because a lot of Republicans did not think this was a good use of time or money. If you’re actually focused on winning the midterms, they wanted to be campaigning in their districts, in their states—let alone for some of them, depending on the district or the state, aligning themselves with a president who’s quite unpopular and whose policies are quite unpopular. But nonetheless, you still saw a number of them travel to Dallas despite not really wanting to, because as Tom said, Trump is the leader of this party and he demanded a midterm convention, so he got one.

Harris: I was, as I was watching it go on, thinking about what was driving the news as we were heading into the convention, which was this sort of burgeoning trade war with Canada.

Trump himself mentioned Canada briefly during the convention, saying—

Donald Trump: Canada very much wants to make a deal. They’re dying to make a deal.

Harris: Tom, that’s all well and good, but the reality is that the president has chosen to squabble with one of America’s closest allies. Where do things stand now between the U.S. and Canada? And is there any sense of a thawing? Or do you think things are continuing to heat up?

Nichols: Well, first, let’s always point out that the president’s default response to any controversy is that Country X is desperate to make a deal. It’s literally Donald Trump’s Mad Lib—one of the Mad Lib sentences. You know, What do you think about the controversy with Country X? The answer is always, Controversy will be over soon. Country X is begging to make a deal. They’re calling me every day, whether it’s Canada, Iran, the Houthis, you name it.

I think the Canadians have simply decided they’ve had enough of this nonsense. They are no longer partners; they are adversaries in the economic space. But I think that the Canadians have said, Fine.

A majority of the Canadians don’t want to pay for this Trump–Carney tariff war, but they support Carney standing up to Trump. And so my guess is this is not retrievable until Trump is gone from office, which is a real tragedy, even if Trump backs down from the tariffs, which he almost certainly is going to do sooner rather than later, I think.

Harris: Yeah. And as you mentioned, right, Carney’s approval rating is quite high. Ashley, how has he been responding to the president, and how has the back-and-forth been going in recent days?

Parker: Well, I sort of understand Carney in his response going back to a speech he gave much earlier this year at Davos, where he basically said, The world order as we—I’m paraphrasing here—the world order as we know it is over. And all of these sort of smaller countries have always supplicated themselves to the United States for protection or for deals or for various reasons, and that’s no longer a good strategy for us. And so I think Carney’s response in this trade war is him sort of acting on those principles he laid out at Davos. And one thing that was so striking to me when you look at the back-and-forth—and it looks like both sides had issues; it’s hard to point specifically to which side blew up the most recent deal—but one thing that comes through is Trump has talked about wanting Canada to be a 51st state, and that mainly seems to be trolling, except not entirely; there’s always a kernel of truth with everything Trump does.

But in these negotiations, it feels like the American side has sort of internalized the idea that Canada is less a sovereign nation and more a 51st state. And when you look at the terms that Canada objected to, it was stuff the United States negotiators demanded, which would be reasonable if Canada was a state, but is not reasonable if Canada is a sovereign nation and an ally to our north. And it feels like that’s where things fell apart.

Harris: Tom, actually in your piece the other day, you talked about the way that the president doesn’t view other nations as sovereign nations. There’s just this idea that he can’t go in and extract things in the way that he would if it were just a part of something that he already owned. Can you sort of flesh out that idea a little bit?

Nichols: Well, I mean, not to psychoanalyze the president from a distance, but I think most people would agree the president’s a pretty narcissistic guy. He’s got to put his name on everything. He builds monuments to himself. Every sentence begins with I. And people like that don’t think of other people as real people; they think of them as players on the stage that surrounds them. And I think that’s very clear with Donald Trump.

This convention, going back to the convention we were mentioning, you know, he doesn’t really think of other people trying to win elections, and he doesn’t care. They’re supposed to come to his big party and wear a hat and bring noisemakers and that’s it. And that’s the extent of his interest. And I think that’s how he is with foreign countries, that he says they’re all kind of wholly or partially owned subsidiaries of Donald Trump Incorporated. He doesn’t think of them as real places with unique cultures or particular interests led by human beings who may not actually see the world the way he does or care about his interests as much as he cares about his interests.

And that’s partly why you always get these kind of stock answers of They’re gonna make a deal, because of course everybody makes a deal, because that’s what I want. And they’re gonna do what I tell them to do, because of course, all my life, everyone has done what I tell them to do.

It flummoxes him completely when a foreign nation says, We’re not going to do that. And one of the reasons—you know, I don’t want to extend this analogy by Canada too far—but I think that’s one of the reasons he’s having such a hard time with the war of choice he began in Iran. He just can’t imagine that—he says, I demand that you do X, Y, and Z. And the Iranians say, No and here’s a bunch of missiles and drones as part of that answer. And I think he totally unravels him, because he’s just never had to deal with that.

And I think when Mark Carney, you know, as Ashley was saying, Who is this uppity governor, to speak to the president in this way?, instead of the leader of a sovereign nation and place that’s part of NATO and has real interests in the world—one of our second or third biggest trading partners. He cannot internalize that. It doesn’t make it—it’s not like he rejects the idea. It’s like he can’t grasp the idea.

Parker: And just to briefly follow on Tom, I mean, Trump has such legitimate faith and confidence in himself as a dealmaker that he really can’t fathom that. You may recall that when he was campaigning, he said, On day one, the war between Russia and Ukraine will end, which is a sort of promise presidents make—day one signals it’s a priority. But in talking to Trump’s aides, they’re like, No, no; he actually thought that. Like, he actually thought that he was such a good dealmaker, it would end. And obviously it hasn’t.

Harris: When we come back, we talk about the danger of AI, and Ashley and Tom talk about what they’ll be reporting on in the week ahead.

[Music]

Harris: I wanna switch gears a little bit, speaking of the idea of things that people can and cannot control. Over the last several days, CEOs of leading AI companies have been sounding the alarm, really in a lot of the same ways that Bill Gates, when he was on the show with Hanna [Rosin] not that long ago, was talking about the growing risks of artificial intelligence and the products and the ways that people are using those products.

Trump doesn’t appear to be heeding those concerns and has responded that the U.S. has to, quote, “win AI.”

What is your reaction to this, to all of this?

Nichols: That’s a classic Trump answer. You know, We have to win AI. That’s the president’s way of saying, I didn’t understand the question. I don’t really know what this is, and so we just have to win it. Because that’s a good kind of standard. You could have filled in anything: What do you think about the, you know, international chocolate-milk market?

Well, we have to win that.

Parker: Yeah, is winning AI, we die first?

Nichols: Yeah. (Laughs.) What does that mean?

Parker: I will confess, I don’t fully understand all of the intricacies of AI either, but from what I do understand, to be somewhat fair to Trump, or to anyone, is that this is just fundamentally incredibly complex. And, you know, lawmakers, one problem you have is if you’ve ever watched these members of Congress—which is basically a gerontocracy—try to get to the bottom of Snapchat or Instagram or social media with teens, right, it’s like they’re speaking a foreign language. And those are table stakes, right? AI is a million times more complicated than posting a problematic video on YouTube or Instagram.

So first of all, a lot of the people in the United States responsible for possibly regulating this are like me, which is terrifying—can’t begin to possibly understand the nuances or the complexities. And the second thing is, even if the United States is willing to regulate, the question is you would sort of need a mutually-assured-destruction pact with China and with other countries. This is a sort of globalized problem.

Nichols: I understand the intricacies very well because I have seen all the Terminator movies. And I know that Skynet is going to become self-aware at some point, and we’re going to regret it.

But to go back to the president’s response, that would have been a more reassuring answer. So that’s a highly complex thing. We want to make sure that we’re handling it responsibly.

And I’m fascinated to know what happened that spooked all of the top, you know, that spooked Altman and Musk and all these other guys. But I’m less of a doomer about it—even if it does scare me. But I think that the first wave of damage, if something like this gets loose, will be economic. But I still don’t know. And, you know, to go back to where we were, I don’t know what it means to win that, other than to say that we will use it to capture more efficiencies than other countries will and put more people out of work faster or something. But I think the danger of this thing is real because the people handling it—I just don’t have a sense that they are looking at this with the kind of civic responsibility that they should have.

Harris: Ashley and Tom, I’m going to ask you to open your notebooks. What questions do you have going into this week? And, Ashley, I’m going to go to you first.

Parker: Sure. So I’m gonna be looking at—I think actually last time I was on your podcast, we were talking about the midterms and why the bottom hasn’t fallen out for the Republicans yet. And, you know, that that was August, but things really kick off after Labor Day. There’s October surprises; voters tune in. I mean, one thing that was fascinating is I talked to someone who does focus groups with swing-state voters who said, You hold up a picture of the Senate candidate in a state, and half the voters don’t even know who he or she is.

So I’m still gonna be asking those similar midterm questions, but at a time when everyone is tuning in and ads land harder; mistakes, gaffs land harder; trying to see where this heads in November.

Harris: And the Republicans are starting to put more of their money into their advertising now. They’re sort of using that war chest we were talking about the last time.

Parker: Yeah, because again, part of this is: They would have liked to have used it earlier. Trump has a lot of money; his groups have a lot of money. But he had to kind of release it. And even if they didn’t spend it, they wanted to get those TV reservations up early because you can get a cheaper rate if you book early.

But the other reason you spend now is because this is when people are paying attention. And Michael Scherer and I spoke to Trump’s pollster Tony Fabrizio, who said at the time when we spoke, he said, Look, yeah, things are bad for the Republicans, but that’s because we haven’t turned to the Democrats yet. The Democrats have a horrible brand, and you should expect to see a ton of contrast ads because elections, as Biden always says, and as everyone understands, They’re a choice.

Nichols: Ashley mentioned, or Adam, I think you mentioned October surprises. And I’m looking for one because when Trump—it gets panicky. I think one of the things I saw at the convention was that he felt very ebullient and energized, but also there was a lot of fear there. He clearly is deeply worried. And when he gets like that, you’re gonna get a surprise of some kind. He’s gonna. And it’s making me wonder what kind of thing will pop. So I guess I’m worried politically about a black-swan event, where he just does something to change the discussion.

The other thing I’m watching, though, is that both in Russia and Iran, these situations are not going away. They are aware that there’s an election impending. And I have to say I don’t know why this is, but late September, early October is always a very fertile time for an international crisis. And I’m concerned that that crisis could erupt either in the Pacific, in Russia, or in Iran, because they’re not on our timetable. They’re not gonna do things on Donald Trump’s timetable or do things based on his interests. And I think all of those places that we’ve stopped watching temporarily because of so much going on at home are percolating, and I’m concerned about what happens next in each of those three, especially in the Ukraine war and in Iran.

Harris: Well, Ashley, Tom, thank you so much for joining me today and helping me sift through the news of the week.

Parker: Thank you for having us.

Nichols: Thanks, Adam.

Harris: That’s all for today’s show.

This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Hadley Robinson. It has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

title: Trump’s See-No-Evil AI Policy
summary: Not long ago, most of Washington was scrambling to be as friendly as possible to the rise of artificial intelligence. Lawmakers from both parties saw a chance to bolster the nation’s economy—and their campaign coffers. But rarely has public opinion flipped so quickly and so thoroughly as it has on A...
content:
Not long ago, most of Washington was scrambling to be as friendly as possible to the rise of artificial intelligence. Lawmakers from both parties saw a chance to bolster the nation’s economy—and their campaign coffers. But rarely has public opinion flipped so quickly and so thoroughly as it has on AI in recent months. While AI was making some tech leaders unfathomably rich, many Americans in states both red and blue grew alarmed by the proliferation of loud, electricity-guzzling data centers, convinced that AI would first make life more expensive and then, for good measure, eliminate their job. In the past few days, some of the top voices in the AI industry have gone further, warning that unless development of the technology is slowed, and slowed soon, all of humanity could be made extinct.

These fears have rattled markets and galvanized a bipartisan set of leaders into calling for the government to step in. AI has now become a central issue in the midterm elections. But President Trump, who first came to power by closely reading the mood of the country and shifting his views to meet those of the electorate, seems to have his fingers in his ears, ignoring it all and continuing to embrace AI, confident that everything will be fine because he is in charge. Unless, of course, the human race ends first.

Trump would seem to have a perfect opportunity to try to contain this fast-moving political conflagration: Next week, he’s set to host China’s president, Xi Jinping, at the White House. The United States and China are the world’s leaders on AI and are in a race to develop the technology. The summit could be a venue, some in the industry hope, to order a pause in development or establish international safety guidelines. But Trump, at least for now, wants no part of a slowdown. AI growth has propped up Wall Street and sectors of the American economy for the duration of his second term, and the president has made clear that he doesn’t want to do anything that could burst that bubble.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on Truth Social today, as he made half a dozen posts, each seemingly more frantic than the last. He later compared the concerns about the technology to his own impeachments, declaring that “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.”

As tech insiders offered warnings about the AI apocalypse, Trump was busy rallying the MAGA faithful in Texas and taking in rounds of golf in Ireland. The dire prophecies began last Tuesday, with a series of viral social-media posts by an AI researcher who said that the technology is advancing so quickly that it could bring about human extinction by the end of the decade. The threat of annihilation seemed to grab Washington’s attention as few other concerns have. By the next afternoon, after several other researchers had echoed the alarm, members of Congress were beginning to call for legislation, new agencies, hearings, and regulations to address the threat. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told us on Wednesday that he had sent invitations to a bipartisan set of lawmakers for a closed-door briefing with AI experts. He said that the researchers had provided a wake-up call about a technology that poses an “extraordinary danger for the human race.” That night, Trump spoke for nearly two hours at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, but he did not mention AI once.

[Read: AI is running laps around our political system]

In the days that followed, more troubling evidence emerged. Anthropic released a report detailing the ways that individuals and nation-states have attempted to misuse its technology, including for sophisticated cyberattacks and research that could potentially support the development of biological weapons.

Trump decamped to Ireland, where he spent the weekend watching a golf tournament at one of his properties. He was dismissive of the Silicon Valley warnings, emphasizing the need to defeat China in the AI race and downplaying the technology’s risks. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote that a downshift in the pace of AI development “could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong.” Other industry leaders joined in, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk, the sometimes–Trump ally.

One of Trump’s first moves upon returning to office last year was to revoke the executive order signed by his predecessor, Joe Biden, that imposed a series of regulations on the AI industry. Trump’s focus was business growth, and he reveled in the power he had over the nation’s tech titans. Many crowded the room at his inauguration, and he has hosted AI-industry leaders such as Altman, former Oracle CEO Safra Catz, and Nvidia President Jensen Huang.

Still, some of Trump’s advisers have had concerns since last year about the political impacts of the AI backlash, when figures as disparate as Sanders and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis began calling for more regulation. To head off the potential populist backlash, Trump announced the Ratepayer Protection Pledge in March, asking major developers of AI to “build, bring, or buy” resources needed for any new electricity-production and utility-infrastructure upgrades. Now the White House is working with House Speaker Mike Johnson to fast-track legislation that would put into law some of the pledge’s voluntary measures. A vote is scheduled for tomorrow.

[From the March issue: America isn’t ready for what AI will do to jobs]

People close to the administration perceive some figures, including White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, to be supportive of additional regulation of the industry, two people familiar with internal White House deliberations told us, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Others, such as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, have advocated for as little government interference as possible, while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has demanded that Anthropic abandon ethical safeguards—such as rules against mass surveillance and autonomous lethal targeting—in its work for the Pentagon. (When Anthropic refused, Hegseth cut ties with the company.)

Trump has dug in on letting AI rip. He has watched as the industry has propelled the stock market, the president’s favorite indicator of a strong economy, keeping it high even amid challenges posed by the Iran conflict, stubborn inflation, and tariffs. Trump has expressed worry to those close to him that a halt to AI expansion could send the economy into a recession, one ally told us.

Some in the president’s orbit have raised suspicions about the AI executives’ warnings: Is this an attempt at market capture? (They worry that new regulations would freeze the industry and prevent would-be competitors from catching up to the industry giants.) Vice President Vance seemed to give expression to that idea by saying today that tech companies “begging the government to regulate them” feels “like a bit of a Trojan horse.” David Sacks, a co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, wondered on social media over the weekend why AI companies cannot just regulate themselves; he told tech leaders to “stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel.” (Top AI firms could work together to implement some safety standards, but antitrust law would likely prevent them from implementing any kind of reciprocal agreement to throttle the pace of development, unless Congress granted a waiver for that purpose, MacKenzie Arnold, the managing director of the Institute for Law and AI, a nonpartisan think tank, told The Atlantic.) Today, Trump called Huang while the CEO was onstage at an AI event to assure the Nvidia head that he will keep supporting the technology.

[Read: J. D. Vance’s AI doctrine]

The pleas for action have created unlikely political bedfellows. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Republican, declared that “we need substantially more regulation,” while Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii, a Democrat, said that Congress needs to “move at the pace of the threat.” Tomorrow, Sanders will join the Trump adviser Steve Bannon at a “Pro-Human Assembly,” an all-day gathering in Washington, D.C., focused on ensuring that humans remain in charge of AI. Despite support for regulation from both the right and the left, there is little meaningful oversight of AI that can be implemented without the president’s approval. Sanders told us that he hopes the bipartisan outrage will ultimately get Trump’s attention. “Trump’s ignorance is extremely dangerous,” he said. “He has not a clue about the dangers inherent in this technology, nor do people in his administration.”

Trump is looking forward to next week’s summit with Xi, which follows a May meeting in Beijing. The U.S. president has stressed his strong relationship with the Chinese leader and has downplayed China’s efforts to thwart the United States. It seems unlikely that Trump will let AI fears fully derail the summit’s agenda. Trump has also minimized China’s chances of catching up to the U.S.—he green-lighted a sale of Nvidia chips to China late last year—even as he has played up the stakes. “Whoever wins AI wins,” he said this past weekend.

But Xi may come into the meeting with a new wariness of his own. China’s top intelligence official warned yesterday that AI could pose a direct threat to the Chinese Communist Party’s hold on power by enabling sophisticated hacking and disinformation campaigns. Many in the industry hope that the summit will be an inflection point. Nate Persily, a co-director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative, told us that “if ever there was an opportunity to get some kind of consensus on AI safety, this provides that opportunity.” And Altman, in an interview over the weekend, made a clever appeal to Trump’s vanity, suggesting that if he and Xi strike some sort of deal to create AI guardrails, the president could win his long-coveted Nobel Peace Prize.

Michael Scherer, Ashley Parker, Will Oremus, and Jack Rodriquez-Vars contributed reporting.

title: How Long Can the U.S. Escape an Atlantic Hurricane?
summary: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.Every president likes to take credit for good news on their watch, but most of them have at least a lit...
content:
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Every president likes to take credit for good news on their watch, but most of them have at least a little shame about it. Not Donald Trump.

September 10 is typically the peak of Atlantic Ocean hurricane season. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expected a relatively restrained year, but as the meteorologist and hurricane specialist Michael Lowry writes, the season “has never gone beyond September 11th in the reliable records (since at least 1950) without a hurricane” in the Atlantic Ocean—until this year. There aren’t even any strong prospects forming.

Amid spreading violence in the Middle East, warnings of an AI apocalypse, and high fuel prices, it’s a rare piece of good news, and Trump wants credit. Over the weekend, the White House flagged the news, commenting, “Thank you, President Trump!” This is absurd, though maybe no one should be surprised that a man who believed that marking a map with Sharpie can change a hurricane’s path would take credit for a low-key storm season. (He also reportedly once suggested attacking storms with nuclear weapons, so perhaps, as the journalist Catherine Rampell jokes, this is deterrence in action.)

Better explanations than presidential benevolence exist. As my colleague Joshua Partlow has reported, this is an unusual year for the El Niño cycle. In the Pacific Ocean, it has produced very warm water, as well as a number of hurricanes. Hawaii, which is seldom hit, has been struck by two hurricanes so far this year. At least four deaths have been attributed to the storms, and power remains out on some parts of the island of Kauai. But scientists say that El Niño also accounts for the absence of major storms, so far, in the Atlantic. “It’s really staggering, just how inhospitable the Atlantic is to anything that could form a tropical cyclone right now,” Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of atmospheric science at the University at Albany, told PBS. The lull is especially notable because last year’s hurricane season was also astonishingly mild in the United States. Although parts of the Caribbean endured hurricanes, not a single one hit the U.S. mainland.

This is great news for the Americans who are otherwise often in hurricanes’ paths, and who have been slammed by a series of storms in the past decade—including 2024’s Hurricane Helene, the deadliest to hit the mainland United States since Hurricane Katrina, in 2005. It is also great news for Trump, who must be one of the luckiest people in history. Hurricanes can help or, more often, badly hurt a president. George W. Bush’s reputation never recovered from Katrina, whereas Barack Obama’s steady hand during Hurricane Sandy seemed to bolster his reelection campaign. Trump’s handling of storms during his first term was poor; he demonstrated little human warmth and, in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria, jarring coldness.

Trump’s personal behavior aside, his administration has been especially fortunate because under his leadership, FEMA appears to be in no shape to handle a major disaster. In the first months of his second presidency, Trump and then–Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced plans to dismantle FEMA entirely, devolving responsibility for relief to states, an idea panned by most experts. In the meantime, he seemed determined to slowly strangle it, appointing interim leaders with no disaster-relief experience. First came Cameron Hamilton, who was fired after telling Congress that he did not support liquidating FEMA. Next was David Richardson, who, shortly after taking his post in May 2025, acknowledged that he had no completed plan for the impending hurricane season and would reuse the previous year’s. (FEMA employees reported that Richardson said he didn’t even realize such a season existed; a FEMA spokesperson later said he was joking.)

Because no storms have since struck the mainland, these failures ended up having much less human and economic cost. FEMA appears to be on a somewhat stronger footing now. Trump has backed off plans to eliminate FEMA, Noem and Richardson are gone, and Hamilton is back as permanent administrator—and has won some tentative praise for working to learn more about disaster relief. He inherits serious challenges, though. A federal judge ruled on Friday that an administration order to lay off half of FEMA’s workforce was illegal. “Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air,” the judge wrote of the government’s proposal, which included cutting thousands of on-call employees who rush in with aid after a disaster.

A report released last month by the Government Accountability Office was even more scathing. The GAO found that FEMA’s personnel decisions had been made “without assessing whether it had the necessary staffing capacity to meet its mission,” including what it is required to do under law, and that “FEMA is not positioned to determine whether it has the right number of people with the right skills in the right positions at the right time to meet its mission.” Furthermore, the report said, “the agency has no overall strategic direction.”

Alas, the calm before the storms won’t last indefinitely. Experts who spoke with The New York Times said that it would be premature to assume that no major Atlantic hurricanes will form this year. If the president’s political luck continues, then perhaps the East Coast won’t see a really bad storm until after the midterm elections, or maybe even next year. Given his administration’s approach to hurricane preparedness and the travails of FEMA, though, ordinary Americans along the Atlantic coast and the Gulf Coast are likely to see their weather luck run out.

Related:

  • This El Niño will be unlike any in the past eight decades.
  • FEMA is not prepared.

Here are four new stories from The Atlantic:

  • Anne Applebaum: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption.
  • Trump’s secret points system for Cabinet members
  • Jonathan Chait: Who needs regulation when Trump is president?
  • Gas prices could cost Republicans the midterms.

Today’s News

  1. President Trump rejected calls for new AI guardrails, saying that the technology instead needs “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” His comments came after several AI executives called for stronger safeguards or a slowdown in development.
  2. New York and 21 other states sued the Trump administration to block a new rule expanding what immigration officials can consider when deciding whether applicants qualify for green cards, visas, or entry into the United States. The rule, set to take effect on Friday, would likely make it harder for people to be approved if officials decide that they would possibly need benefits such as Medicaid, food assistance, and housing aid.
  3. A second federal judge blocked the Trump administration’s new mail-ballot rules, finding that the Postal Service likely lacks the authority to impose them. The Supreme Court will weigh in on the rules ahead of the November elections.

Dispatches

  • The Wonder Reader: Isabel Fattal explores what asking for help does for the people helping.

Explore all of our newsletters here.

Evening Read

Illustration by Matteo Giuseppe Pani / The Atlantic

The Biggest Obstacle to Universal Child Care: Babies

By Kendra Hurley

Last year seemed like a pretty big one for breakthroughs in child care. In New York City, Zohran Mamdani’s promise of publicly funded care for young kids helped him win the keys to Gracie Mansion. Officials in Connecticut created an endowment to make care more affordable in that state. And New Mexico became the first state to commit to free child care for all of its residents. But as policy makers have begun hammering out the details of these ambitions, they’ve hit against a stubborn and formidable obstacle: babies.

Read the full article.

title: Trump’s Kennedy Center Shakedown
summary: The saga of Donald Trump’s repeated attempts to slap his name onto the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts will not go away. In May, Trump lost in court and was ordered to remove his name from the building. But now—according to a 57-page presentation by Trump’s hand-picked executive board...
content:
The saga of Donald Trump’s repeated attempts to slap his name onto the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts will not go away. In May, Trump lost in court and was ordered to remove his name from the building. But now—according to a 57-page presentation by Trump’s hand-picked executive board obtained by The Washington Post—the Kennedy Center is warning that it will likely go bankrupt. Unless, that is, Trump gets to put his name back on the wall next to that of his slain predecessor.

The Post reports:

Trump’s support hinges on getting public credit for his involvement. The financial resolution says Trump has offered to “raise the necessary funds to keep the Center from bankruptcy” while the building undergoes a sweeping renovation. But it says Trump is unlikely to provide “fundamental oversight” of that project or lead a financial rescue without “appropriate recognition” of his role.

That’s not an offer of help; it’s a shakedown—or, in more direct terms, political blackmail. Two lawyers who have been fighting the Trump administration, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, said in a statement: “Trump is taking the Center hostage and threatening to in effect kill it unless he gets his way.” The president is counting on the board’s civic spirit and affection for the institution—neither of which he evidently possesses—to strong-arm it into giving him what the law and courts would not allow.

Even more galling than Trump’s attempt to pressure the trustees is that his offer is a response to a crisis mostly of his own creation. It’s true that the Kennedy Center, opened more than a half century ago, needs investment and repairs. But the plummeting ticket sales are a result of Trump’s hostile takeover. Performers and patrons alike did not want to legitimize the obscenity of placing Trump’s name on an institution meant to honor Kennedy, and they voted with their feet and their dollars. This very public repudiation of Trump by a slice of the American cultural elite appears to have been an embarrassment to the president; Trump then claimed that he needed to close the center for two years (ostensibly for a complete reconstruction) rather than suffer further humiliation.

(Trump, apparently, could not submit to the public indignity of having his name removed from the building in June. He—or someone seeking to please him—ordered workers to cover the building’s wall with tarps at 3 o’clock in the morning so that no one would see the removal. The tarps remain in place.)

[Read: Dead-mall vibes at the Kennedy Center]

The only way to avert letting the center go bankrupt, according to the executive board, is to let Trump raise money—and heaven knows what kind of ethical issues that effort would entail—and then to add his name to thank him. The presentation to the board suggests 10 possible statements to place on the building, including “Renovation Restoration and Endowment overseen by President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Putting Trump’s name in front of Kennedy’s is an especially offensive touch, and would enshrine the idea that the center would no longer be named solely for Kennedy.

The American people do not support Trump’s mania for renaming things, of which the Kennedy Center is just one example. (The White House itself has become a public exhibit of Trump’s garish taste, including gold script identifying The Oval Office, as if it’s a function room at one of his resorts that needs to be labeled in case a tipsy wedding guest gets lost.) All of this architectural bombast and glitz are expressions both of ego and of insecurity: Trump wants to leave his mark—and his name—on a city that has never accepted him and that will almost certainly try to scrub away his influence when he is gone.

The president admitted as much recently, when the writer Ben Terris asked him whether he is building monuments to himself because he is worried that no one else will build them when he’s gone. “That’s true,” Trump said. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will.”

The president’s admission suggests a way to deal with his attempted shakedown of the Kennedy Center board: take his dare.

[Read: The Kennedy Center has a problem that courts can’t fix]

The center’s top officials, the people who were supposed to be entrusted with the future of this cultural icon, have admitted their failure. They acknowledge that Trump will not support the institution unless his name is on it. Well, so be it. The trustees should let the center close, declare bankruptcy, and come to a sad end—all on Trump’s watch. Allow the Kennedy Center to fail in full view of the American public, and let them decide whether such things matter.

Otherwise, Trump will plow ahead and do something no one wants, because no one bothered to stop him.

The Kennedy Center can always be rebuilt and reopened. Indeed, the restoration of the center could be one of the items on the next president’s to-do list. Scrap the czarist-style ballroom. Rebuild the East Wing of the White House. Halt the fascist-flavored victory arch that will dishonor nearby Arlington Cemetery. Fix the Reflecting Pool. Chisel Trump’s name off the U.S. Institute of Peace. (If the president wants to land at Donald J. Trump International Airport in Palm Beach when he leaves office, that’s between him and the people of Florida.) Painful as it would be to see the Kennedy Center go bankrupt, it would be more painful to cave to Trump’s deeply cynical refusal to save a national treasure unless he gets his name on it.

In a famous 1911 poem that gave the world another name for blackmail—danegeld, a reference to the protection money that medieval English villages paid, often in vain, to Danish raiders—Rudyard Kipling warned powerful countries against caving to extortionary threats. The Kennedy Center board, and the American people, should heed Kipling’s advice:

We never pay any-one Dane-geld,

   No matter how trifling the cost;

For the end of that game is oppression and shame,

   And the nation that plays it is lost!

title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
summary: St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved AfricansInside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemora...
content:
St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans

Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.

The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.

Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirds

The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering.

If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth.

content:
Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South Africa

Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m through online romance scams were extradited to the United States on Friday.

South African police confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, while local news in Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa.

content:
Her Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globally

Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.

The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.
